Private DNS resolves `bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` to those ENI IP addresses. The following Figure 21 shows the removal of subnet association.\\\\n\\\\n*[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/5b384ce32d8cdef02bc3a139d4cac0a22bb029e8/2026/04/17/NetCDNBlog-1723-image-21.gif)Figure 21: Modify subnets associated with interface VPC endpoint*\\\\n\\\\nWhen someone removes both subnet associations, the ENIs are deleted. The endpoint still exists and Private DNS still resolves the hostname to the endpoint, but there is nothing to handle the traffic. This is the scenario that is particularly hard to spot by hand, because the console still shows the endpoint as \u201cAvailable\u201d even though requests time out with no response. It is worth noting the difference between the two endpoint types: VPC Gateway Endpoints (Amazon S3, Amazon DynamoDB) work through route table entries and endpoint policies, so a misconfiguration there returns an Access Denied (HTTP 403 Forbidden) error. Interface VPC Endpoints (Amazon Bedrock and many other AWS services) work through ENIs in your subnets with their own security groups, so when those ENIs are gone, you get connection timeouts instead. But the database still works (VPC local route), Amazon S3 still works (VPC Gateway Endpoint has its own route table entry), and outbound internet connectivity still works (NAT Gateway route is intact). Only the Bedrock AI check turns red.\\\\n\\\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/5b384ce32d8cdef02bc3a139d4cac0a22bb029e8/2026/04/17/NetCDNBlog-1723-image-22.png)*Figure 22: Simulated workload application status page*\\\\n\\\\nDevOps Agent receives the `BedrockAccessFailures` alarm and investigates:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Checks endpoint configuration** \u2013 Finds zero subnet associations on the Interface VPC Endpoint.\\\\n2. **Searches CloudTrail logs** \u2013 Finds the `ModifyVpcEndpoint` API call, including who removed the subnet associations\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/automated-network-incident-response-with-aws-devops-agent/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Use AWS PrivateLink to set up private access to Amazon Bedrock | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## Set up the VPC endpoint for Amazon Bedrock\\\\n\\\\nIn this section, we use Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) to set up the VPC endpoint for Amazon Bedrock to facilitate private connectivity from your VPC to Amazon Bedrock.\\\\n\\\\n1. In the **Subnets** section, and select the Availability Zones and choose the corresponding subnet IDs from the drop-down menu.\\\\n\\\\n7. For **Security groups**, select the security group with the group name `Bedrock-GenAI-Stack-VPCEndpointSecurityGroup-` and description `Allow TLS for VPC Endpoint`.\\\\n\\\\nA security group acts as a virtual firewall for your instance to control inbound and outbound traffic. Note that this VPC endpoint security group only allows traffic originating from the security group attached to your VPC private subnets, adding a layer of protection.\\\\n\\\\n8. Choose **Create endpoint**.\\\\n9. {"id": "e1fa9d34-20bd-40f3-b5ed-7dbde31499c1", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I couldn't find a documented "VPC endpoint check" for Bedrock, so I can't give you a severity for it. I searched AWS documentation twice and found no AWS-published check or control for Bedrock VPC endpoints with a severity attached. I'd rather say that than make up a finding and a rating.

**Where the check probably comes from.** If your assessment tool reports a severity, the check is defined by that tool. Examples are Prowler, a Security Hub CSPM standard, a Config conformance pack, or a custom scanner. Which tool are you running, and what's the check ID or name? The exact wording and severity will be in its rule definition or in the finding itself.

**What AWS documents about the setup.**
- Private connectivity to Bedrock uses interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). The service names include `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime`, and there are others for the control plane and agents.
- Interface endpoints put ENIs in your subnets and are governed by security groups and an optional endpoint policy.
- Having only the default VPC and no Bedrock endpoint means Bedrock calls from that VPC would go over the public service endpoint. That's usually through an internet gateway or NAT, not over PrivateLink.
- That is a hardening gap, not a vulnerability. Whether it counts as a finding, and how severe, depends on the tool and on your policy. Many tools rate it low or informational unless you require private-only access. Treat that as general context, not as what your specific check reports.
- The check's result may also depend on whether any workloads in that region actually run in the default VPC. A region where Bedrock is called only from outside AWS, or from a VPC other than the default one, could be handled differently.

If you give me the tool and check name, I can look up its documented behavior. I can also check read-only whether any Bedrock endpoints exist in that region, by listing the VPC endpoints there and filtering for `bedrock` service names.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

**Where the check probably comes from.** If your assessment tool reports a severity, the check is defined by that tool. The exact wording and severity will be in its rule definition or in the finding itself.

**What AWS documents about the setup.**
- Private connectivity to Bedrock uses interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). The service names include `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime`, and there are others for the control plane and agents.
- Interface endpoints put ENIs in your subnets and are governed by security groups and an optional endpoint policy.
- Having only the default VPC and no Bedrock endpoint means Bedrock calls from that VPC would go over the public service endpoint. That's usually through an internet gateway or NAT, not over PrivateLink.
- That is a hardening gap, not a vulnerability. Whether it counts as a finding, and how severe, depends on the tool and on your policy. Many tools rate it low or informational unless you require private-only access. Treat that as general context, not as what your specific check reports.
- The check's result may also depend on whether any workloads in that region actually run in the default VPC. A region where Bedrock is called only from outside AWS, or from a VPC other than the default one, could be handled differently.
